claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating is initially face-centered cubic.
The initial FeNiCrCoCu lattice has high lattice distortion.
Co, Cr, and Ni in the FeNiCrCoCu coating can exhibit thermally activated magnetic fluctuations.
Raising temperature induces longitudinal spin fluctuations that alter magnetic entropy and internal-energy contributions.
Increasing temperature raises stacking-fault energy through magneto-volume coupling.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations significantly increase the stacking-fault energy in FeNiCrCoCu.
Higher stacking-fault energy suppresses stacking-fault and nanotwin formation.
Higher stacking-fault energy suppresses partial-dislocation emission.
Suppression of partial dislocations, stacking faults, and twins causes dislocation starvation.
Above 900 K, deformation changes from dislocation-mediated plasticity to localized amorphization.
Thermal expansion and magnetic entropy fluctuations destabilize the fcc lattice.
Loss of stacking-fault-mediated accommodation causes rapid lattice disorder and amorphization under indentation.
The amorphous layer has high friction because it lacks shear localization.
Structural collapse of the amorphous layer causes rapid loss of wear resistance.
At 900 K and 1200 K, the coefficient of friction increases sharply while hardness and wear resistance drop precipitously.
High-temperature failure is accompanied by an increase in HCP-classified atoms or amorphous atoms in the deformation zone.
At 600 K, dislocation density decreases while the lattice remains crystalline.
At 300 K, dislocation motion is the primary deformation mode.
Stable oxide films can reduce friction in AlCoCrFeNiTi at high temperature.
The oxide-film-dominated behavior in AlCoCrFeNiTi occurs at 900 K.

contradictions.description: The proposed transition is repeatedly restricted to temperatures above 900 K, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule treat the transition as occurring at 900 K itself.

The mechanism predicts suppression of stacking faults and twins, which normally produce HCP signatures in an fcc lattice, while the predicted outcome allows an increased HCP atom count as a signature of the same transition. HCP and amorphous counts need to be treated separately to avoid this ambiguity.
